How our family pickle business survived the lockdown

My grandmother started making mango pickle in our kitchen in 1987. She sold it to neighbours in steel tiffin boxes. Over the years the business grew slowly. By 2019 we had a small unit with eight workers and a delivery van. Then the lockdown came in March 2020. For three weeks we could not open the unit at all. Our workers were worried about their salaries. My father decided to pay them from our savings. We started taking orders on WhatsApp from families in our colony. My younger brother delivered them on his scooter. It was hard work, and some days we made a loss. Slowly, people began to share our number with their relatives. Orders came from other cities, so we learned how to pack jars for courier. The first few parcels leaked and we had to refund two customers. We switched to thicker jars and sealed lids. Today we sell on BONC and ship to twelve states. My grandmother still tastes every new batch. She says the secret is patience, not spices. We are grateful to every customer who trusted us in those difficult months.

Five things I learned in my first year as an exporter

When I started exporting handmade rugs, I knew nothing about documentation. The first lesson was that every buyer asks for samples, and samples are expensive. I now charge for samples and adjust the cost against the first order. The second lesson was about payment. One buyer delayed payment for four months, and it almost stopped my production. Since then I work with letters of credit for new buyers. The third lesson was about quality. A small colour difference between the sample and the order led to a big argument. Now I share photos of every lot before dispatch. The fourth lesson was about freight. Rates change every week, so I never promise a fixed freight price for more than seven days. The fifth lesson was about patience. Some buyers take months to reply, and that is normal. I made many mistakes this year, but each one taught me something. My advice to new exporters is simple. Start small, keep your promises, and write everything down. The market rewards people who are reliable more than people who are cheap.

A visit to a cotton farm in Vidarbha

Last month our team visited a cotton farm near Wardha. We wanted to see where our yarn really begins. The farmer, Mr. Deshmukh, has been growing cotton for thirty years. He showed us his fields and explained the sowing season. The rains were late this year, and he was worried about the crop. Pests are a big problem, and he has to spray several times. He told us that input costs have doubled in ten years. His son now uses a phone app to check prices at the mandi. We sat with his family and had lunch under a neem tree. The children asked us many questions about the city. On the way back we talked about how little we knew about farming. Our yarn prices depend on people like Mr. Deshmukh, but we rarely think about them. We have decided to buy part of our cotton directly from farmer groups. It will take time to set up, but it feels like the right thing to do. We will share our progress in a future article.

Why our factory switched to LED lighting

Two years ago our electricity bill was higher than our rent. Most of it came from old tube lights and halogen lamps. An energy auditor visited our unit and measured every machine. He found that lighting used almost a quarter of our power. We replaced three hundred fittings with LED panels over two weekends. The workers noticed the difference immediately. The shop floor was brighter and cooler. Fewer lights failed, so the maintenance team had less work. Our bill fell by eighteen percent in the first month. The investment paid for itself in about fourteen months. We also installed motion sensors in the store rooms. Some people worried that the sensors would switch off lights while they were working. We adjusted the timers, and now nobody complains. Small changes like this add up over the years. Next we plan to install a rooftop solar plant.

My daughter's first science fair

This is not a business story, but I wanted to share it. My daughter is eleven years old and loves plants. For her school science fair she decided to test which fertiliser works best for tomatoes. She planted twelve seedlings in old paint buckets on our terrace. Every morning she measured them with a ruler and wrote the numbers in a notebook. Some plants died in the heat, and she cried the first time it happened. We told her that failed experiments also teach us something. She kept going and even made a graph on the computer. On the day of the fair she was very nervous. The judges asked her many questions, and she answered all of them. She did not win first prize, but she got a special mention. She was a little disappointed on the way home. Then she asked if she could try again next year with chillies. I think that is the best result we could have hoped for.

Understanding GST on job work

Many small manufacturers do job work for bigger companies. The GST rules for job work confuse a lot of people. In simple terms, job work means processing goods that belong to someone else. The principal sends the materials with a delivery challan, not a tax invoice. The job worker charges GST only on the service, not on the full value of the goods. The goods must come back within one year for inputs and three years for capital goods. If they do not come back in time, the principal must treat it as a supply. Keeping good records is the most important thing. Every challan should match the goods received and returned. Our accountant checks these records every month. Mistakes can lead to notices from the department, which take time to resolve. If you are unsure, speak to a chartered accountant before signing a job work agreement. The rules change from time to time, so always check the latest notifications. This article is general information and not legal advice.
